## 1.2 Soundness of the Proposed Methodology (Including Interdisciplinary Approaches, Consideration of the Gender Dimension and Other Diversity Aspects, and the Quality of Open Science Practices)

### The fundamental methodological commitment: uncertainty propagation as the non-negotiable architectural invariant

The overarching methodological commitment of this project is the Uncertainty Chain (METH-CORE-004, source_grounded, concept_note.md): every coupling point in the observation-to-decision pipeline must pass distributional information rather than collapse it to a scalar. This is not a stylistic preference but a principled epistemological position. A probabilistic decision framework that collapses uncertainty at any coupling point — converting a posterior distribution over the field state to a point estimate before passing it to the crop simulation, or calibrating AquaCrop to a single overconfident parameter set rather than retaining a parameter posterior — cannot claim honest uncertainty propagation. It adopts the vocabulary of a probabilistic framework while delivering the overconfidence of a deterministic one. The Uncertainty Chain is simultaneously the project's architectural invariant and its primary verifiable scientific claim: the validation protocol (OBJ-3, WP3) will test directly whether the reported uncertainty is honest by checking whether stated prediction intervals have their nominal empirical coverage across held-out ground-truth observations. A calibration failure at this test is a scientifically valid finding the design explicitly accommodates and would report transparently. The integrity of the chain is therefore testable and falsifiable, not merely asserted.

This architectural stance governs every model and calibration choice in the framework:

Candidate model families for Route A — Direct Probabilistic Fusion (METH-ROUTE-001, source_grounded, concept_note.md) — are restricted to those that intrinsically return full distributions over the target field state rather than point estimates. The named candidate families are Bayesian hierarchical models and Gaussian processes (concept_note.md, source_grounded). Both are epistemic: Bayesian hierarchical models encode prior beliefs about the data-generating structure through hierarchical hyperpriors and update on observations to produce a full posterior; Gaussian processes encode prior beliefs about smoothness through kernel functions and produce a posterior Gaussian distribution over the latent function. Both return not just a predicted value but a probability distribution over the latent field state — root-zone soil moisture, crop water stress, canopy condition — given all available observations. Frequentist regression methods returning point estimates with large-sample confidence intervals under specific distributional assumptions are not structurally equivalent for the chain's purposes: they do not produce a posterior that can be propagated as a distribution into the next stage.

AquaCrop calibration (METH-DEC-002, source_grounded, concept_note.md) is performed retaining an explicit parameter posterior rather than converging to a single best-fit parameter set (T2-01, WP2; wp_structure.json, source_grounded). Standard deterministic crop-model calibration minimises a loss function to produce one parameter set, which is then held fixed — introducing no representation of parameter uncertainty into subsequent simulations and effectively breaking the uncertainty chain at the soil-water-plant interface. Retaining the posterior means each simulation run samples from both the field-state posterior passed from the diagnostic branch and the AquaCrop parameter posterior, producing output variability that correctly represents the combined uncertainty from both sources. The calibration approach builds on a prior peer-reviewed method (doi:10.1016/j.envsoft.2022.105556, referenced in concept_note.md as 'the fellow-attributed method'; PI Role, METH-PART-003, Inferred from first-person authorship of the design narrative) that demonstrated uncertainty-preserving AquaCrop calibration with a deterministic field-state input. The fellowship extends the approach upstream — accepting an uncertain field-state posterior from the diagnostic branch as the calibration input — and downstream — passing the combined parameter-and-state uncertainty into the counterfactual simulation layer.

Counterfactual irrigation simulation (METH-DEC-003, METH-DEC-004, source_grounded, concept_note.md) runs AquaCrop over a weather-scenario ensemble rather than a single assumed weather trajectory (T2-02, WP2; wp_structure.json, source_grounded). Running over a single trajectory would produce a point estimate of the yield consequence of each candidate irrigation decision, discarding all weather uncertainty. Running over the ensemble produces a distribution of economic outcomes per candidate decision, enabling the profit-based recommendation to integrate over genuine joint weather-and-model uncertainty rather than optimising against assumed weather certainty. The ensemble is the mechanism through which prospective uncertainty — the economic consequence of irrigation decisions depending on weather that has not yet occurred — is made computationally tractable.

### Underlying assumptions: explicitly named and empirically tested rather than silently buried

The framework rests on four structural assumptions. Each is explicitly named and either empirically testable during the project or handled by the two-route switching mechanism.

Assumption A1 — Covariate informativeness. Route A assumes the available covariates — Sentinel-1 SAR, Sentinel-2 optical, in-situ soil sensors, weather data and field observations — carry sufficient information about the latent field state to support posterior inference. This is justified by precedent in the systematic literature review (METH-SOTA-001, source_grounded, concept_note.md): Bayesian Maximum Entropy drought fusion, the MF-FusionNet multimodal architecture, and dynamic Bayesian network crop-water-state modelling collectively demonstrate that multi-sensor covariates carry enough information about soil moisture and water stress to support probabilistic inference in related problem settings. The assumption is empirically testable during WP1: if the posterior variance over the field state remains extremely wide regardless of observations, the covariates are uninformative and the assumption fails. The failure mode is detectable and scientifically valid as a negative finding.

Assumption A2 — Route B patch covariation. Route B (METH-ROUTE-002, source_grounded, concept_note.md) assumes that a nearby spectrally homogeneous patch whose biology covaries with the target crop provides a usable clean-pixel proxy. This is the route's principal assumption. It is explicitly not accepted on faith: a pre-registered quantitative covariation test (RQ9, Confirmed as open, confirmation_checklist.json; Control Stand Variant, METH-ROUTE-003, source_grounded, concept_note.md) will measure, rather than assume, the biological covariation. The Control Stand Variant strengthens this test further by deliberately planting a covarying species in the proxy patch, enabling controlled longitudinal measurement of covariation over the growing season rather than inference from opportunistic observations. If the pre-registered test fails, the framework reverts to Route A as the primary diagnostic route without redesigning WP2, WP3 or WP4 — the route-switching contingency (RISK-05 mitigation, Inferred, risks.json) requires no structural change to the shared decision engine.

Assumption A3 — AquaCrop representativeness. The framework uses the FAO AquaCrop model (METH-DEC-001, source_grounded, concept_note.md) as the crop physiology interface for the prognostic branch. This assumes AquaCrop's soil-water-canopy parameterisations are adequate for the target crop in the target environment. AquaCrop is FAO's validated, mechanistically grounded crop simulation model specifically designed for water-limited conditions and calibrated in peer-reviewed literature for a wide range of crops. The specific crop is open scientific decision RQ1 (Confirmed as open, confirmation_checklist.json; default: horticultural row crops). Parameters are calibrated empirically during the fellowship using the uncertainty-aware calibration approach rather than adopted from generic tables, which limits the exposure to any specific parameterisation mismatch.

Assumption A4 — Weather ensemble representativeness. The counterfactual simulation runs over a weather ensemble whose composition is assumed to represent the relevant distribution of near-term weather outcomes for the growing season window. The specific weather data provider is Unresolved (DATA_PROVIDERS, confirmation_checklist.json); no fabricated weather ensemble specification is asserted. The ensemble design is part of the technical design space that will be resolved once the data provider is confirmed.

### The two-route architecture as systematic and symmetric methodological risk management

Route A and Route B (METH-ROUTE-001, METH-ROUTE-002, source_grounded, concept_note.md) are not a primary method and a fallback. They are two credible scientific paths to the same methodological output type — a field-state posterior with explicit uncertainty — that share the same downstream decision engine, the same validation protocol, and the same uncertainty-calibration framework. Whether one or both are implemented as the primary method, and whether one serves as a comparison benchmark or a genuine scientific alternative, is open scientific decision RQ2 (Confirmed as open, confirmation_checklist.json). The symmetric interchangeability is a structural design property rather than a post-hoc rescue option.

The two routes address the same core methodological challenge from different angles. The sub-pixel resolution problem (METH-SOTA-003; Downscaling Critique, source_grounded, concept_note.md) arises because coarse satellite pixels over heterogeneous fields aggregate signals from multiple land-cover types, and decomposing that aggregated signal back to sub-pixel field-state estimates introduces disaggregation error on top of any model's intrinsic uncertainty. Route A sidesteps this entirely: it treats the multi-sensor covariate vector as input to a single probabilistic model that goes directly from observations to the latent field state in one step, with no intermediate pixel-level product to disaggregate. There is no disaggregation step, so no disaggregation error is added. Route B sidesteps it differently: by selecting a nearby spectrally homogeneous patch the coarse satellite pixel can read cleanly without any sub-pixel mixture, it eliminates the aggregation problem at source — the pixel it reads is already homogeneous. Both routes therefore avoid the disaggregation error source characteristic of approaches that produce intermediate sub-pixel land-surface products before estimating the field state.

The two routes also manage complementary model-complexity risks. Route A's rigorous one-step probabilistic fusion over a high-dimensional, heterogeneous covariate space may impose demanding computational and modelling-expertise requirements that exceed what is feasible within a 24-month fellowship [DURATION — Unresolved, confirmation_checklist.json; operator-declared 24 months under SYN-SPINE-01, working_assumptions.json; to be confirmed]. This is RISK-07 (Inferred, risks.json): if Route A exceeds available compute or modelling capacity (T1-02, WP1; wp_structure.json), Route B delivers OBJ-1's required output independently. Route B's covariation assumption failure (RISK-05, Inferred, risks.json) is its symmetric risk; the contingency is reverting to Route A. The two risks are complementary — the primary risk factor for one route is the other route's contingency — which is the structural basis for describing the architecture as risk-managed by construction rather than by hope.

### Four disciplines, three coupling points, and the necessity of interdisciplinary integration

The methodological design necessarily integrates four disciplines. Each discipline is authoritative at one stage of the pipeline, and no subset of fewer than four can close the full observation-to-decision chain.

**Earth observation remote sensing.** ESA Sentinel-1 SAR and Sentinel-2 optical data (METH-INFRA-002, source_grounded, concept_note.md; freely available open Copernicus data) provide the primary observation layer. Earth observation science governs satellite sensor characteristics, geometric registration, atmospheric correction, temporal compositing across observations with different overpass frequencies (Sentinel-1: approximately 6-day repeat; Sentinel-2: approximately 5-day repeat), and cloud-masking routines to handle optical data gaps during cloud cover periods (RISK-03, Inferred, risks.json; SAR is cloud-penetrating and compensates for optical gaps). Without this disciplinary grounding, the sensor-preprocessing pipeline (T1-01, WP1; wp_structure.json) would produce miscalibrated inputs to the probabilistic model, introducing systematic biases that would manifest as miscalibration in the posterior and contaminate the uncertainty chain from its first stage.

**Probabilistic machine learning.** The diagnostic branch (WP1, T1-02, T1-03; wp_structure.json) requires probabilistic ML expertise to specify informative prior distributions over the latent field state, design efficient posterior inference algorithms (variational inference, Markov Chain Monte Carlo, or sparse GP approximations for scalability), implement the heterogeneous-sensor covariate pipeline that handles asynchronous multi-sensor inputs at different spatial and temporal resolutions, and diagnose posterior calibration. Without probabilistic ML expertise, the multi-sensor observations cannot be fused into a principled distributional estimate of the field state — the model would either be a deterministic retrieval algorithm (losing the uncertainty chain at stage one) or an ad hoc ensemble (producing poorly calibrated uncertainty). The extension in WP2 (T2-01; uncertainty-aware AquaCrop calibration) requires probabilistic ML expertise applied to a crop-model parameter inference problem: posterior inference over AquaCrop's soil-crop parameters conditioned on available yield, phenology and soil moisture observations from the validation site.

**Crop physiology and agricultural hydrology.** AquaCrop (METH-DEC-001, source_grounded, concept_note.md) is the crop simulation model at the WP1–WP2 interface (Diagnostic Branch to Decision Engine). AquaCrop's mechanistic representation of the soil-water-plant-atmosphere continuum requires crop physiology expertise to parameterise correctly for the target crop: canopy development dynamics, root deepening rates, biomass water productivity coefficients and water stress response functions are physiological quantities that must be set from agronomic knowledge and calibrated empirically, not inferred by a probabilistic algorithm without crop-science context. The uncertainty-aware calibration approach (METH-DEC-002, source_grounded) builds calibration uncertainty around the physiological parameters rather than treating them as known constants; this requires crop physiology knowledge to specify which parameters are most uncertain given the available calibration data, and probabilistic ML knowledge to design the posterior inference. Without crop physiology, the probabilistic model cannot simulate how a diagnosed water-stress state leads to a yield outcome under different irrigation decisions; without that simulation, the decision engine has no basis for ranking candidate irrigation options.

**Agricultural economics.** The profit-based decision objective (METH-DEC-005, METH-DEC-006, source_grounded, concept_note.md) frames irrigation choice as expected-profit maximisation — expected crop value minus full irrigation costs — across the weather ensemble rather than yield maximisation alone. Agricultural economics provides the objective function specification and the conceptual framing of the irrigation decision as an economic problem under uncertainty. A crop-physiology-only objective would maximise yield; this ignores the cost of irrigation water and energy, the market price of the crop, and the asymmetric cost of overwatering relative to underwatering in different crop-price scenarios. The profit-based framing explicitly treats underwatering risk (yield loss) and overwatering risk (cost overrun) as commensurable economic losses, enabling the framework to identify the decision that maximises expected economic return across the distribution of weather outcomes. Without agricultural economics, the decision engine would produce recommendations that are agronomically sound but economically suboptimal for farming practitioners. The exact decision objective is open scientific decision RQ6 (Confirmed as open, confirmation_checklist.json; default framing: expected crop value minus costs); the framework is architected to accommodate any scalar scoring function over the simulation output distribution without requiring structural redesign.

**Why an interdisciplinary approach is necessary and not optional.** An approach confined to any single one of the four disciplines cannot close the observation-to-decision chain. A pure Earth observation approach without probabilistic ML cannot produce distributional uncertainty estimates over the field state. A pure probabilistic ML approach without crop physiology cannot simulate the economic consequences of irrigation decisions given a diagnosed field state. A pure crop physiology approach without agricultural economics cannot identify the profit-maximising option as distinct from the yield-maximising option. A pure agricultural economics approach without multi-sensor Earth observation cannot diagnose the field state required to initialise the simulation. The interdisciplinary integration is not a cross-disciplinary enrichment of a single-discipline approach but a structural requirement: each discipline is irreplaceable at one stage of the pipeline, and no stage can be satisfied without it. The coupling points — EO preprocessing to probabilistic ML fusion; probabilistic posterior to AquaCrop calibration; AquaCrop simulation distribution to economic decision criterion — are where the disciplines meet and where specific, technically demanding design decisions must be made jointly. The research programme at WP1 (EO × Probabilistic ML; T1-01, T1-02, T1-03) and WP2 (Probabilistic ML × Crop Physiology × Agricultural Economics; T2-01, T2-02) embodies this structural interdisciplinarity in its task decomposition.

### Gender dimension and other diversity aspects in the research and innovation content

The gender dimension question is addressed in relation to the project's research and innovation content — the algorithms, models, validation design and demonstrator interface — not team composition.

At the level of the project's core technical procedures, the probabilistic inference algorithms (Bayesian hierarchical model, Gaussian process), the AquaCrop soil-water-plant simulation, the counterfactual weather-ensemble approach, and the profit-based economic objective function are mathematically defined procedures applied to geophysical and agronomic observations. These procedures compute the same result regardless of the gender, ethnicity, or other demographic characteristics of the farming practitioner whose field is being monitored or whose irrigation decisions are being supported. The mathematical-procedural core is gender-neutral in the sense that its computations do not condition on demographic variables.

However, at two boundaries of the research design, gender and diversity considerations are substantively relevant to methodological choices that are within the project's scope to influence:

First, at the validation data collection boundary (OBJ-3, WP3, T3-01; wp_structure.json, source_grounded). The validation protocol collects ground-truth data at field sites with farming practitioners. Row-crop horticulture involves diverse farming populations in which gendered divisions of labour, land tenure patterns, and decision-making authority over irrigation decisions vary across cultural contexts, farm sizes and geographic settings. The methodology of ground-truth collection — specifically who provides the field observations, on whose fields the measurements are made, whether the data-collection instruments (field survey forms, sensor installation protocols) are equally accessible to all demographic groups of farming practitioners, and whether the validation sample is demographically representative of the farming population the framework is designed to serve — has direct consequences for the generalisability of the framework's performance claims. A validation data set collected exclusively from one demographic group of farmers cannot support a performance claim generalising to all row-crop farming practitioners. These design elements fall within the ground-truth definition (RQ4, Confirmed as open, confirmation_checklist.json; T3-01, WP3) and will be addressed in the validation protocol specification. The validation sites and data providers are Unresolved (DATA_PROVIDERS, confirmation_checklist.json) and the protocol cannot be fully specified until they are confirmed. The methodological importance of demographic representativeness in validation sampling is noted here as an open design requirement that the protocol must address, not as a completed commitment.

Second, at the demonstrator accessibility boundary (OBJ-4, WP2, T2-03; wp_structure.json, Inferred, synthesis). The standalone research demonstrator presents probabilistic irrigation recommendations — distributions over economic outcomes per candidate decision, not point estimates — to a user audience of farming practitioners with varied levels of statistical literacy, varied digital access and varied educational backgrounds. Communicating honest probabilistic uncertainty to non-specialist users is a research-communication design challenge that, if not addressed, would make the demonstrator's outputs accessible only to farming practitioners with formal quantitative training. The design of uncertainty communication — how prediction intervals, probability distributions and expected values are displayed in the web MVP interface — is a diversity-of-access problem: if the demonstrator is readable only to users with a statistical background, it systematically excludes the majority of the farming practitioners it is designed to serve. This applies across multiple dimensions of diversity — educational background, digital literacy, language — not only gender. Demonstrator accessibility is a design criterion for the web MVP and is within the fellow's scope to operationalise during T2-03. Structured engagement with diverse user groups during demonstrator development — potentially through the validation partner network (VALIDATION_PARTNER, Unresolved, confirmation_checklist.json; to be specified once the partner is confirmed) — is the mechanism through which this criterion can be empirically addressed rather than assumed.

In summary, the gender dimension and other diversity aspects are not directly relevant to the mathematical-procedural core of the methodology (probabilistic inference, crop simulation, economic optimisation) but are substantively relevant at the validation data collection and demonstrator accessibility layers — both of which are active research design questions within the project's scope. The honest position is not that gender is irrelevant but that gender and diversity considerations apply at the knowledge-production and knowledge-use boundaries of the project's methodology, not at the mathematical core, and that the open design questions at those boundaries (RQ4, TRL target and interface design within RQ10) are the methodological site at which these considerations must be operationalised.

### Open science practices as integral methodological requirements, not administrative obligations

Open science is a methodological requirement for this project's central scientific validity claim, not a parallel compliance activity. The framework's defining claim — that its reported prediction intervals are calibrated, that is, that a stated 90% prediction interval contains the truth approximately 90% of the time — cannot be accepted or rejected by the scientific community unless the framework is fully inspectable. A black-box demonstration producing apparently calibrated predictions cannot be distinguished from a system that has been tuned to pass the specific validation test used. Third-party reproducibility of the calibration finding requires that the probabilistic model implementation, the AquaCrop calibration module, the counterfactual simulation engine, the validation data and the protocol specification be publicly available and independently deployable. Open science is therefore the external validity condition for the framework's primary scientific claim, not an optional enrichment.

**Data Management Plan (Deliverable D5-01; Milestone MS1, month 6).** The DMP (T5-01, WP5; wp_structure.json, source_grounded) is delivered by month 6 as a mandatory scope requirement (SR-06 / CC-10, CC-11, scope_requirements.json, Confirmed). Its month-6 delivery is deliberately timed before the peak data-intensive phases: the Diagnostic method v1 milestone (MS2, month 12, Confirmed, milestones_seed.json) and field validation (WP3, starting month 8). The DMP is not a retrospective data catalogue but a prospective data design specification: it defines from the project's inception the data format standards, metadata schemas, version-control procedures, access conditions, long-term repository arrangements and licensing terms under which all project data will be collected, stored and published under FAIR principles — Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable. Writing the DMP before the sensor pipeline is built (WP1, T1-01) constrains the pipeline design to produce outputs that are in principle reusable by third parties: the format and metadata schema decisions made at DMP stage propagate into the data engineering decisions made at pipeline-build stage. This front-loading of data design is methodologically important: retro-fitting FAIR compliance to a pipeline that was designed without it is more costly and often incomplete. The DMP contributes to expected outcome EO-07 (Stronger R&I capacity and output; better transfer of knowledge, Confirmed, expected_outcomes.json; Confirmed mapping, concept_refinement_summary.json) through the structured, FAIR-compliant data assets it defines, and is a direct delivery against SR-06's requirement to foster Open Science culture and prepare the fellow for FAIR data management.

**Open research software: the diagnostic and decision engine implementation.** The probabilistic diagnostic model (Route A and/or Route B; WP1, T1-02, T1-03), the uncertainty-aware AquaCrop calibration module (WP2, T2-01), the counterfactual irrigation simulation and decision engine (WP2, T2-02), and the standalone research demonstrator (WP2, T2-03) will be developed as open-source software under FAIR-compliant open licences. Open-source software is the necessary condition for third-party inspection of the uncertainty quantification implementation. The chain's calibration claim — that uncertainty is propagated without collapse through the coupling points — can be verified empirically only if a third party can run the same implementation on the same data. A closed-source implementation makes this impossible; even if the paper reports calibration results honestly, the community cannot verify that the described procedures were implemented as described. Open-source development follows standard best practices: version-controlled public repository with documented releases, automated unit tests covering the probabilistic inference components, and usage documentation sufficient to enable independent deployment. The open research software outputs contribute to EO-03 (Enhanced networking and communication capacities with scientific peers, Confirmed, expected_outcomes.json; Inferred mapping, concept_refinement_summary.json) by enabling peer review of the implementation alongside the scientific publication, and to EO-07 (Stronger R&I capacity, Confirmed) by making the implementation reusable by subsequent crop-water modelling research programmes.

**Open validation data and reproducible validation protocol.** The field validation (WP3, T3-01, T3-02) produces two open-science outputs: the ground-truth data collected at the validation site(s) (subject to confirmation of DATA_PROVIDERS, Unresolved, confirmation_checklist.json) and the complete validation protocol specification (ground-truth definition per RQ4; uncertainty-calibration metrics and coverage test per RQ5; pilot-success criteria per RQ7; patch-covariation pre-registered test per RQ9). Publishing ground-truth data under FAIR principles alongside the software implementation enables full replication of the calibration finding: an independent researcher who downloads the published software, applies it to the published data using the published protocol, and reports the resulting coverage metric has executed a valid replication. This standard of reproducibility is what the framework's central scientific claim demands. The validation data publication is planned as a component of MS5 (Field validation and uncertainty calibration complete, due month 22, Confirmed, milestones_seed.json) and is governed by the DMP's data management provisions from MS1.

**Open-access publication.** At minimum one open-access peer-reviewed publication covering the probabilistic fusion-to-decision framework is targeted by MS6 (month 24, Inferred, milestones_seed.json). Open access satisfies the Findable and Accessible dimensions of FAIR for the scientific results, ensuring the primary contribution is reachable by farming practitioners, research communities and policymakers in regions without institutional subscription access. The publication strategy is a component of the WP5 dissemination and exploitation plan (T5-02; wp_structure.json) and contributes to EO-03's enhanced networking and communication capacities.

**Open science as the training vehicle for research integrity and FAIR data stewardship (SR-06, CC-10, CC-11, scope_requirements.json, Confirmed).** Designing and maintaining the FAIR DMP (D5-01), developing open-source software with version control, documentation and automated tests, designing the validation protocol for third-party reproducibility, and preparing open-access publications are not activities run in parallel with the research. They ARE the research. Writing the DMP requires active decisions about data provenance, format and accessibility that directly shape how the sensor pipeline (T1-01) is engineered. Designing the validation protocol for reproducibility requires decisions about what ground truth is collected and how it is documented that directly shape what WP3 measures. Developing open-source software with tests and documentation requires continuous attention to code correctness and modularity that directly shapes the reliability of the uncertainty chain implementation. The research-integrity and open-science-ethics dimension of the MSCA-PF mandatory transferable-skills training (SR-06) is therefore not a separate training module appended to the research programme but an integral discipline practised through every primary research task. This integration of open science as methodology rather than compliance is the most defensible position for a framework whose scientific claims rest on third-party reproducibility.
